paragraphs: Since no rule requires a site to operate a quality system (Gap 1), Section 3.5 placed the justification of the framework in the origin of each of its parts. Sections 4.2 to 4.5 gave that origin instrument by instrument, but a site deciding whether to adopt the framework would raise a different objection, because it already keeps many records and a set of well-founded forms can still leave a problem unread. A site can note an unplanned component substitution in the operative note and again in the device accountability record, and the substitution can recur in later cases until a monitor finds it, since nobody at the site read the two records together. The framework therefore has to be justified as a whole in two ways. Its records have to connect, so that a record made in one place reaches a decision in another, and its parts have to be complete and necessary, so that every domain has a control and every instrument has an origin. Table 4.3 lists the twenty-four instruments by pillar, with what each one reads, what it produces, and the section and appendix where it is developed.

Information moves through the three levels of Figure 4.3, and each instrument works at one of them. At the lowest, a record holds the evidence of one event or one person, such as one procedure in the ICDL or the release of one person in the TRE. Above it, a synthesis reads several records together, such as the learning curve log for one surgeon or the follow-up review for one period. At the top sit the decisions about how the site runs, from the delegation matrix to the risk register, and they rest on those syntheses. Information rises through the levels, and a decision returns to the lowest one as the requirement that the next record is checked against. In a site that runs the full set, the substitution above takes this path. The ICDL records it in the operating room, the learning curve log reads it in the sequence of that surgeon's cases, and the indicator of surgeon procedural consistency reports it for the period. If the pattern holds, the PI records a decision in the POT, which may return the surgeon to proctoring through the credentialing record, and from then on the ICDL of that surgeon's cases is checked against the new condition. The event is recorded under Operational Controls, read under Risk Management and Performance Oversight, and decided under Governance, which is why the instruments were designed only after the functions of all four pillars had been defined.

Only five instruments ask for work at the clinical moment, the PSEAR, the ICDL, the IQL, the PFVR, and the SART, and they sit where Chapter 3 placed the data that cannot be recovered once lost. The other nineteen work on records that already exist, either those five or the clinical records of the site, so the set meets DR11 and the rule on source documentation. The same division explains why the minimum sets of Section 4.7 still close the loop. In a smaller set, the synthesis that a dedicated instrument would carry, such as the learning curve log or the indicators of the PIR, falls to the oversight meeting held under the POT, while the records of the clinical moment stay at every level, four of them as instruments and the visit record through its proxy. A smaller site therefore gives up the dedicated reading of a signal and keeps the evidence that would show it. How much periodic work the nineteen represent for a small team has not been measured.

Figure 4.4 gives the justification that Section 3.5 asked for. It crosses the twenty-four instruments with the twelve CtQ domains in its upper part and with the twelve design requirements in its lower part, with a filled marker where an instrument carries the control of a domain or answers a requirement directly and an open marker where it supports one carried elsewhere. Across the full set, every domain has at least one filled marker, and so does every requirement that an instrument can answer on its own, so no domain is left to a general duty and no requirement is left without an instrument. Every column also has a filled marker in one of the two parts, so no instrument is in the set without a domain it controls or a requirement it answers. Some instruments enter from one side only. The DTRM and the TRE answer no requirement on their own and enter through the control of training (domain 6), and the PFVR and the FUCR enter in the same way through follow-up and endpoint assessment (domains 7 and 8). DR9, DR11, and DR12 describe the set as a whole and run across the lower part as one bar each. DR9 is met by the phase that Figure 4.2 assigns to every instrument, and DR11 and DR12 by the way the set is used, since the instruments work through the documentary system of the site and the minimum sets of Table 4.2 keep at every level the records that the regulations require.

The figure also separates the two kinds of control that Section 3.5 distinguished. Domains 5, 6, 8, and 9 rest wholly or partly on requirements that none of the regulatory texts examined assigns to the site, and their filled markers fall on instruments of the site's own, from the credentialing record and the learning curve log to the ICDL and the imaging records, most of which answer DR3, DR6, or DR7 directly. These are the controls the framework adds to what the regulations ask of the site. In the other domains the filled markers fall where the regulations already place a duty on the site, such as the delegation of tasks or the reporting of adverse events, and there the framework organizes work the site already owes.

The map also shows where control is thin. Consent rests on the eligibility record alone, because the regulations already set its process in detail and Chapter 3 gave it no requirement beyond the risk register. Endpoint assessment is the thinner case, since its control rests on the visit record and the follow-up review, while the qualification and consistency of the assessor, which the domain also covers, sit in the training records. When the endpoints of an investigation depend on readings that vary between observers, the site therefore adds the training requirements matrix on the basis of its risk register, as Section 4.7 describes. The figures show that the records are designed to connect and that each part has an origin, and they cannot show that a site reads what it records in time to act, which is the question Section 5.4 takes up.

Draft templates for all twenty-four instruments are in Appendices A to X. They were developed for shoulder device investigations, and their content reflects that context mostly in the complication categories and the imaging requirements, and also in the complexity levels of the learning curve log. Their structure, from the fields to the review triggers and the escalation logic, was kept as general as that context allowed, so adapting an instrument to another surgical specialty would in most cases mean changing its classification lists, although no such adaptation has been tested. The templates are provided in an open, editable format, so a site can match them to the layout of its own documents and add or remove fields, while the function that each instrument carries stays the same.
